Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Mumbai, India at 2026-02-12 12:30 IST (UTC+0530) (2026-02-12T07:00:00Z in UTC), at latitude 19.076 degrees and longitude 72.8777 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 56.797 degrees and its azimuth is 169.915 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 16.173 degrees and its azimuth is 230.855 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 25.16 percent illuminated, 60.074 degrees from the Sun, and 401170.4 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To give you an honest estimate: **No, you almost certainly will not be able to see it.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the specific data you provided:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Factor
The most significant hurdle is the Sun's position. You noted the Sun is at an altitude of **56.8 degrees**. This means the Sun is very high in the sky, creating intense "sky glow." 

Even though the Moon is technically above the horizon (at 16 degrees), it is currently in the "daytime" part of its cycle. At 25% illumination, the Moon is a thin crescent. Because it is so close to the Sun in the sky (only 60 degrees apart), it is sitting in the brightest part of the atmosphere. The scattered sunlight in the air will completely overwhelm the faint reflection of light off the Moon's surface.

### 2. The Moon's Phase and Position
A 25% illuminated crescent is relatively "thin." While a Full Moon can sometimes be seen during the day (though it looks like a faint ghost), a crescent Moon is much harder to spot because it has very little surface area reflecting light toward you. 

Furthermore, with an azimuth of **230.8°** (South-West) and the Sun at **169.9°** (South-South-East), the Moon is trailing the Sun. It is high enough to be "up," but it is not low enough on the horizon to be shielded by the thickness of the atmosphere in a way that would make it stand out against the blue sky.

### 3. The "Ordinary Eyesight" Constraint
Since you are using unaided eyesight, your pupils will be constricted due to the bright daylight. This significantly reduces your ability to see low-contrast objects. To see the Moon in these conditions, you would need a pair of high-powered binoculars or a telescope to "isolate" the Moon from the surrounding glare of the sky.

### The Verdict
If you were to look toward the South-West, you would see a very bright, blue, washed-out sky. You might see some high-altitude clouds or perhaps a very bright planet (like Venus, if it were in the right position), but the Moon will be invisible to the naked eye.

**Probability of spotting it: < 1%**
